'''Gerhard Hessenberg''' ({{IPA|de|ˈɡɛʁhart ˈhɛsn̩ˌbɛʁk|lang}}; 16 August 1874 – 16 November 1925) was a German [[mathematician]] who worked in [[projective geometry]], [[differential geometry]], and [[set theory]].

==Career==
Hessenberg received his [[Ph.D.]] from the [[University of Berlin]] in 1899 under the guidance of [[Hermann Schwarz]] and [[Lazarus Fuchs]].

His name is usually associated with [[projective geometry]], where he is known for proving that [[Desargues' theorem]] is a consequence of [[Pappus's hexagon theorem]],<ref>
{{Citation
| last = Hessenberg
| first = Gerhard
| title = Beweis des Desarguesschen Satzes aus dem Pascalschen

| year = 1905
| url = http://www.digizeitschriften.de/dms/img/?PID=GDZPPN002260638
| mr = 
| zbl =
| doi= 10.1007/BF01457558
| s2cid = 120456855
| url-access = subscription
}}.
</ref> and [[differential geometry]] where he is known for introducing the concept of a [[Connection (mathematics)|connection]].<ref>
{{Citation
| last = Hessenberg
| first = Gerhard
| title = Vektorielle Begründung der Differentialgeometrie
| language = German
| journal = [[Mathematische Annalen]]

</ref><ref>[http://scienceworld.wolfram.com/biography/Hessenberg.html Hessenberg, Gerhard (1874-1925)] from Eric Weisstein's World of Scientific Biography</ref> He was also a set theorist: the [[Ordinal arithmetic#Natural operations|Hessenberg sum and product]] of [[ordinal number|ordinal]]s are named after him.  However, [[Hessenberg matrix|Hessenberg matrices]] are named for [[Karl Hessenberg]], a near relative.

In 1908 Gerhard Hessenberg was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Rome.<ref>{{cite book|author=Hessenberg, G.|chapter=Zaehlen und Anschauung|pages=377–379|volume=3|title=Atti del IV Congresso internazionale dei matematici (Roma, 6–11 Aprile 1908)|chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=iau.31858027749682;view=1up;seq=399}}</ref>
